cues.text: Counting begins by defining an outcome.
If you choose one shirt, one pair of trousers and one pair of shoes, an outfit
is the complete triple of choices.
With two shirts, three trousers and two shoe options, there are two times
three
times two, or twelve outfits.
This multiplication rule works because each partial choice admits the stated
number of next choices.
It does not require probability independence.
If restrictions make that number vary, split into cases or count each branch
separately.
The addition rule combines disjoint alternatives.
If a journey uses either one of four train services or one of three bus
services, and the services are distinct options, there are seven choices.
You add because taking one service is the outcome; you are not taking a train
and then a bus.
If cases overlap, simple addition double counts the shared outcomes.
Remove that overlap or rewrite the cases so each outcome belongs to exactly
one.
A small tree diagram is useful: branches represent successive choices, and
completed paths represent outcomes.
Before using a factorial or a combination symbol, say whether you are
selecting, ordering or performing several stages.
Suppose seven distinct runners compete for first, second and third positions,
with no ties.
A podium is an ordered list of three different people.
There are seven choices for first, six for second and five for third, giving
two hundred ten podiums.
This is the permutation count P of seven, three.
For n distinct objects placed into r ordered positions without replacement,
multiply n by n minus one, continuing for r factors.
In factorial notation the result is n factorial divided by n minus r
factorial.
A factorial multiplies positive integers down to one, and zero factorial is
defined as one.
This is consistent with one empty arrangement when no positions are filled.
Arranging all n distinct objects gives n factorial.
Choosing zero positions gives one outcome, not zero.
The formula assumes r is an integer between zero and n.
If more distinct objects are requested than are available without replacement,
there are no such arrangements.
When repetition is allowed instead, each position may have n choices and the
count becomes n to the power r.
Always attach the replacement rule and the meaning of positions to the
formula.
A selection of three people with no assigned roles is a different outcome from
a ranked podium.
A committee of three chosen from seven distinct people has no ranking among
its members.
Listing the same three names in a different order does not create a different
committee.
The permutation count two hundred ten counts each committee three factorial
times, because its members can occupy the three list positions in six orders.
Divide by six to obtain thirty five committees.
In general, C of n, r equals n factorial divided by r factorial
times n minus r factorial.
The relation P of n, r equals r factorial times C of n, r explains the
distinction between selection and arrangement.
Selecting r people is also equivalent to specifying the n minus r people left
out, giving C of n, r equal to C of n, n minus r.
Pascal's identity follows by fixing one distinguished person.
A committee either contains that person and chooses its remaining r minus one
members from the others, or excludes that person and chooses all r from the
others.
The cases are disjoint.
Thus C of n, r is C of n minus one, r minus one plus C of n minus one, r.
For choosing three from seven, this gives fifteen plus twenty, again thirty
five.
Repeated symbols change the meaning of an arrangement.
The word BANANA contains six letters: three copies of A, two copies of N and
one B.
If every physical copy were temporarily labelled, six factorial orders would
be
possible.
Removing labels makes each visible arrangement occur three factorial times
from
the A labels and two factorial times from the N labels.
Divide by both factors to obtain sixty distinct strings.
More generally, with n objects divided into indistinguishable types of
multiplicities n one, n two and so on, the count is n factorial divided by the
product of the multiplicity factorials.
The multiplicities must sum to n.
For A, A, B, the visible strings are AAB, ABA and BAA, agreeing
with three factorial divided by two factorial.
Do not divide by a factorial merely because two objects share a broad
description if the problem treats those objects as distinct.
Two named students remain distinct even if they wear identical uniforms.
Conversely, labelling identical balls changes a distribution problem.
The right divisor comes from how many labelled outcomes collapse to each
visible outcome.
Check that this number is constant before using division as a shortcut.
This keeps repeated object reasoning connected to the actual objects being
counted.
Adjacency constraints often become simpler when a group is treated as one
block.
Five distinct people, including A and B, stand in a row.
If A and B must be adjacent, combine them into one block.
Along with the other three people, this makes four units to arrange, giving
four factorial orders.
Inside the block, A B and B A are two different orders.
Multiply to obtain forty eight rows.
If three specified people among the same five must all stand consecutively,
the
block and two remaining people form three units.
There are three factorial outer orders and three factorial internal orders,
giving thirty six rows.
The phrase together must mean consecutive positions for this construction.
It does not automatically mean a fixed internal order; that needs a separate
condition.
If a particular order A before B is required within their two person block,
only one internal order remains.
Blocks may also fail when several adjacency requirements overlap, so draw the
intended pattern before multiplying.
A useful check for the two person example is that all five person rows number
one hundred twenty.
The forty eight adjacent rows form a subset, leaving seventy two rows where A
and B are separated.
We will recover that separated count with gaps.
To keep two specified people apart in a five person row, arrange the other
three people first.
There are three factorial anchor orders.
Each anchor row has four gaps: before the first person, between consecutive
people and after the last.
Put the two special people into different gaps, choosing two of the four gaps
in six ways.
Then decide which special person uses which chosen gap in two ways.
The result is six times six times two, or seventy two rows.
Each valid row has a unique anchor order and choice of occupied gaps, so no
row
is counted twice.
This agrees with subtracting the forty eight adjacent rows from all one
hundred
twenty rows.
The same method handles four distinct anchors and three distinct special
people
when no two specials may be neighbours.
Four factorial anchor orders give five gaps; choose three gaps and arrange the
three specials, giving four factorial times C of five, three times three
factorial, or one thousand four hundred forty.
If specials are indistinguishable, remove their internal arrangement factor.
If several may share a gap, the simple different gap formula is unavailable.
The wording of the separation condition determines which placement pattern is
valid.
Circular arrangements require an equivalence convention.
Suppose six distinct people sit around a round table, with rotations treated
as
the same seating and reflections treated as different.
Fix one chosen person as the reference position.
The other five can be placed clockwise in five factorial orders, giving one
hundred twenty circular seatings.
This removes the rotational overcount that would appear if we numbered all six
starting positions.
If the chairs are labelled, rotations change which labelled chair each person
occupies, so there are six factorial seat assignments instead.
Do not automatically divide by another factor of two: clockwise and
anticlockwise orders are different under the stated convention.
Necklaces or bracelets can use different conventions, especially when repeated
objects create additional symmetries.
Those require a separate analysis.
If A and B among the six people must be adjacent, treat them as a block.
The block plus the other four people gives five units around the table.
Fix a reference unit to count four factorial circular orders, then multiply by
two internal block orders, obtaining forty eight.
Always name the objects, decide whether chairs are labelled, and state whether
reflection is identified before selecting a circular counting formula.
The formula follows from those choices rather than from the word circle alone.
A digit string and a three digit number need not have the same count.
Using zero, one, two, three and four without repetition, a three digit number
has four choices for its first digit because zero is excluded.
After choosing a nonzero first digit, four digits remain, including zero, for
the second position.
Three remain for the third.
The total is forty eight.
A length three code allowing an initial zero instead has five times four times
three, or sixty possibilities.
If repetition is allowed for a three digit number, the count is four times
five
times five, or one hundred.
To count even three digit numbers without repeated digits, split by the final
digit.
If it is zero, the first digit has four choices and the middle digit three,
giving twelve.
If the last digit is two or four, there are two choices for that last
position.
The first digit must exclude zero and the chosen last digit, leaving three
choices.
Then three digits remain for the middle position, giving eighteen.
Add the disjoint cases to obtain thirty.
Filling a constrained position first often makes the available choices easier
to track.
State the digit set and repetition rule throughout the argument.
A committee usually records who belongs, not the order in which names were
chosen.
From five distinct women and four distinct men, the total number of three
person committees is C of nine, three, or eighty four.
To require at least one woman, subtract the committees containing only men.
There are C of four, three, or four
of those, leaving eighty committees.
The complement condition none is simpler than adding separate cases for one,
two and three women.
For exactly two women and one man, choose two from the five women and one from
the four men.
Multiply ten by four to obtain forty committees.
Now suppose any three people may form a committee, but one of them must be
designated chair.
Choose the committee in eighty four ways and choose its chair in three ways,
giving two hundred fifty two outcomes.
Equivalently, choose the chair first in nine ways and the other two members
from the remaining eight in twenty eight ways.
The results agree because they describe the same final outcome.
If several distinct roles are assigned, record which person fills each role.
A committee with a chair is different from a committee with no roles, even
when
the same people belong to it.
A distribution problem must say whether the objects and boxes are
distinguishable.
Consider five identical balls placed into three labelled boxes, allowing an
empty box.
An outcome is completely described by nonnegative integers x, y and z whose
sum
is five.
Write five stars and insert two bars to split them into three groups.
A group may be empty, so bars may be adjacent or occur at either end.
Choosing the two bar positions among seven total positions gives C of seven,
two, or twenty one distributions.
This is the stars and bars argument for a finite nonnegative integer solution
count.
If every box must receive at least one ball, place one ball in each box first.
Two balls remain to distribute without restrictions.
There are C of four, two, or six possibilities.
Equivalently, positive x, y, z become one plus three new nonnegative
variables.
If the five balls were distinct instead, each independently chooses one of the
three labelled boxes, giving three to the fifth power, or two hundred forty
three assignments when empty boxes are allowed.
Neither count applies automatically to unlabelled boxes.
Before choosing a formula, state the object types, box labels and lower bounds
so the combinatorial model matches the question.
